objectives.objective: Configure CLAUDE.md files with appropriate hierarchy, scoping, and modular organization
keyPoints: Hierarchy: user-level (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md), project-level (.claude/CLAUDE.md or root CLAUDE.md), and directory-level files in subdirectories.
User-level instructions are never shared via version control — team conventions there silently miss teammates and new hires.
`/memory` shows exactly which memory files loaded; it is the first diagnostic when behaviour differs across sessions or machines.
Keep configuration modular: @import external standards files, and organize topic-specific rules in .claude/rules/ rather than one monolith.
Directory-level CLAUDE.md scopes conventions to a subtree; personal always-on preferences belong at user level.
objectives.watchFor: A monolithic CLAUDE.md makes every session pay the token cost of standards that do not apply, and unrelated conventions bleed into the current task.

question.stem: One developer's Claude Code sessions follow the team's conventions; a new hire's do not, on the same repo. What is the most likely cause?
options: The new hire's Claude Code version predates the conventions file
The conventions live in the first developer's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, which is not shared through version control
The project CLAUDE.md exceeds the context budget and is being truncated
The new hire needs to run /memory to load the project conventions
question.answerWhy: User-level memory is personal and never travels with the repository, which is the classic cause of conventions that work on one laptop only — moving them to a version-controlled project file fixes it. A version mismatch or truncation would not correlate with the individual developer, and /memory is the diagnostic that reveals the loaded files rather than a command that loads missing ones.

objectives.objective: Create and configure custom slash commands and skills
keyPoints: .claude/commands/ in the repo is shared with the team; ~/.claude/commands/ is personal and never leaves the machine.
Skills live in .claude/skills/ as directories containing SKILL.md, whose frontmatter is the control surface.
context: fork runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context so verbose or exploratory output does not pollute the main conversation — only the result returns.
allowed-tools restricts what the skill may do; argument-hint prompts for required parameters at invocation.
Personal variants of a shared skill go in ~/.claude/skills/ under a different name.
objectives.watchFor: Universal coding standards must not be a skill — on-demand invocation means they silently don't apply in every session where nobody invokes it. Always-on standards belong in CLAUDE.md.

question.stem: A codebase-analysis skill produces thousands of lines of intermediate output, exhausting the main conversation's context. Which frontmatter setting addresses it?
options: allowed-tools, restricting the skill to read-only operations
context: fork, so the skill runs in an isolated sub-agent context and returns only its result
argument-hint, so the developer narrows the analysis scope at invocation
Moving the skill from .claude/skills/ to ~/.claude/skills/
question.answerWhy: context: fork exists precisely for verbose or exploratory skills: the work happens in an isolated context and only the distilled result comes back to the main conversation. allowed-tools bounds capability rather than context, argument-hint collects inputs, and changing the skill's scope affects who can run it, not how much context it consumes.

objectives.objective: Apply path-specific rules for conditional convention loading
keyPoints: Rule files in .claude/rules/ take YAML frontmatter with a paths field of glob patterns; the rule loads only when matching files are edited.
Two benefits: no irrelevant context in sessions that never touch matching files, and deterministic path-driven loading rather than the model inferring which section applies.
Globs follow file type across the tree (**/*.test.tsx for co-located tests); directory-level CLAUDE.md follows location.
One rule file can scope to multiple trees via a list of globs; use recursive globs (dir/**/*) for whole subtrees.
Universal standards stay in CLAUDE.md — rules are for genuinely scoped conventions.
objectives.watchFor: A glob written for a layout the codebase does not have (scoping tests to src/tests/** when tests are co-located) silently never loads, and leaving the text in root CLAUDE.md after migrating it double-loads content that then drifts.

question.stem: Test files named Button.test.tsx are co-located beside their components throughout the codebase, and testing conventions should apply whenever one is edited. What is the best mechanism?
options: A rule file in .claude/rules/ with paths: ["**/*.test.tsx"]
A directory-level CLAUDE.md in each directory containing tests
The testing conventions in the root CLAUDE.md so they always apply
A skill that developers invoke before working on tests
question.answerWhy: The convention follows file type rather than location, so one glob-scoped rule matches those files wherever they live and loads deterministically only when relevant. Directory-level files would mean duplicating and synchronizing the same text everywhere a test lives, root CLAUDE.md pays the token cost in every session, and a skill applies only when someone remembers to invoke it.

objectives.objective: Determine when to use plan mode vs direct execution
keyPoints: Plan mode: large-scale changes, multiple valid approaches, architectural decisions, multi-file modifications — explore safely and produce a design before committing changes.
Direct execution: single-file, well-understood changes with clear diagnostics, where planning overhead buys nothing.
Signals for plan mode: microservice restructuring, a migration touching 45+ files, competing integration approaches with different infrastructure requirements.
The modes combine — plan the investigation-heavy phase, then execute the committed plan directly.
Isolate verbose discovery in the Explore subagent and keep only summaries in the main context.
objectives.watchFor: Reflexive plan mode on trivial fixes adds ceremony that erodes the team's willingness to plan when it actually matters — and direct execution on unmade architectural decisions produces half-migrated code.

question.stem: A team must integrate a payment provider, and two viable approaches differ in their infrastructure requirements. How should the work start?
options: Direct execution on the approach the team prefers, adjusting as issues surface
Plan mode to explore the codebase and select an approach, then direct execution to implement the committed plan
Plan mode throughout, including the implementation of each file change
Direct execution on both approaches in parallel branches, then compare
question.answerWhy: Unmade architectural decisions with differing infrastructure implications are the canonical plan-mode signal, and once the approach is committed direct execution implements it efficiently. Starting with direct execution lets a mid-implementation discovery invalidate completed work, plan mode does not modify code so it cannot carry the implementation, and building both approaches fully doubles the cost of a decision planning can settle.

objectives.objective: Apply iterative refinement techniques for progressive improvement
keyPoints: Inconsistent interpretation of a transformation → give 2–3 concrete input/output examples; a real pair settles ambiguity no stricter prose resolves.
Edge cases like null handling are fixed fastest with specific test cases: example input, expected output.
Test-driven iteration: write the suite first covering behaviour, edge cases, and performance, then iterate by sharing failures.
Unfamiliar domain where you cannot yet specify expected behaviour → interview pattern: have Claude ask you questions before implementing.
Interacting issues go in one detailed message; independent issues iterate better sequentially.
objectives.watchFor: Responding to every miss with longer, sterner prose loops indefinitely on the same misinterpretation — examples are what disambiguate.

question.stem: A data-migration script keeps splitting a composite field differently on each attempt, despite increasingly detailed prose instructions. What is the most effective next step?
options: Provide two or three concrete input records with their exact expected output
Rewrite the instruction with stricter, more precise wording
Write the full test suite first and iterate on failures
Ask Claude to interview you about the migration requirements
question.answerWhy: Concrete input/output pairs resolve exactly the ambiguity that prose keeps failing to pin down, because the expected result is shown rather than described. A stricter rewrite repeats the approach that already failed, a full test suite is heavier than needed here, and the interview pattern is for domains where you cannot yet state the expected behaviour — which is not the case.

objectives.objective: Integrate Claude Code into CI/CD pipelines
keyPoints: -p (--print) makes Claude Code process the prompt, write to stdout, and exit — without it the CI job hangs waiting for interactive input.
For machine-consumable output use --output-format json with --json-schema; a prompt-level "respond in JSON" instruction is probabilistic.
CLAUDE.md carries project context — testing standards, fixture conventions, review criteria — into CI-invoked runs, raising output value.
Provide existing test files so generation doesn't duplicate coverage the suite already has.
On re-runs, include the prior review's findings and ask only for new or still-unaddressed issues.
objectives.watchFor: Letting the session that generated the code review its own changes wastes the benefit of context isolation — an independent instance reviews more effectively.

question.stem: A CI review job hangs until timeout, and when it did run its free-form output broke the script that posts inline PR comments. What fixes both problems?
options: Add a timeout to the CI step and a regex parser for the output
Invoke with -p for non-interactive execution and use --output-format json with --json-schema for parseable findings
Add a system prompt instruction to respond only in JSON and exit when finished
Run the job in a container with stdin closed so the session terminates
question.answerWhy: -p is what makes Claude Code run non-interactively and exit, and CLI-level JSON output with a schema gives the consuming script a contract instead of prose to scrape. A timeout plus regex treats both symptoms, prompt-level formatting promises eventually break automation, and closing stdin is an indirect hack that leaves the output shape unspecified.
